item.title: Hegseth's treatment of lawmakers threatens Trump's $1.5 trillion defense plan
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
This summer, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asked a Republican lawmaker what he thought the odds were that Congress would pass the Trump administration’s record $1.5 trillion defense budget request. The chances, the lawmaker responded, were about the same as Hegseth getting confirmed again by the Senate. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “You have a problem, and you need to increase the amount and the quality of the communication” with Congress, the Republican lawmaker recounted in an interview, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe the private exchange. Months later, members of both parties said the Pentagon has not changed course. For decades, defense issues have mostly remained insulated from Washington’s toxic partisanship. But Republicans and Democrats say they increasingly fear that fire wall no longer exists. With just over 20 legislative days left in the year - and next week’s election likely to empower Democrats eager to confront Hegseth - lawmakers are deadlocked on their major defense policy and spending bills. Failure would leave the Pentagon with few options to replace the thousands of weapons spent during eight months of war with Iran and halt the administration’s ambitious military agenda. To understand how the consensus collapsed, The Washington Post spoke with 30 people at the center of national security in Congress, including 20 lawmakers who sit on the committees that oversee the Pentagon and its budget. Republicans argued that Democrats are stalling critical military funding to placate voters incensed at President Donald Trump. Democrats framed their opposition as a necessary check on an administration that the GOP-controlled House and Senate have refused to hold accountable for starting a war without the approval of Congress. But most lawmakers who spoke with The Post described the impasse in more personal terms. Hegseth’s adversarial behavior - from withholding information to attacking Democrats and some Republicans - was straining the bipartisan dealmaking that has long ensured support for the military, members of both parties said. “The people who have been around for a few days have seen what normal looks like,” Rep. Joe Courtney (D-Connecticut) said. “We’re not living in normal.” In a statement, Pentagon spokesman Joel Valdez defended Hegseth’s approach, saying the secretary is “always willing to engage directly with any lawmakers who bring forward their concerns in good faith.” “Lawmakers understand exactly how critical the National Defense Authorization Act and defense appropriations are to military readiness,” Valdez said, referring to the pending bills. “We do not expect them to deliberately cripple the force or our warfighting capability simply to score political points.” The collapse of bipartisanship The NDAA is widely considered a must-pass bill. The legislation, which covers issues from troop pay to weapons production, has advanced for 65 consecutive years. A similar, albeit less reliable, coalition helps pass the annual defense spending bill, which provides the money to pay troops, buy weapons and conduct military operations worldwide. The group of Republicans and Democrats who typically support the legislation has fractured this year. The NDAA failed to advance in the Senate and barely passed the House, where more Republicans voted against it than Democrats voted for it. The two chambers are negotiating a final version with votes expected later this fall. At greater risk of failing, most lawmakers said, is the annual defense budget. The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion plan would fund a range of advanced weaponry, from commercial-style drones to precision missiles depleted during the Iran war. It directs billions more toward some of Trump’s personal projects for the military, including a Golden Dome missile defense shield, a fleet of battleships named after him and renaming the Defense Department as the “War Department.” Hegseth has called the 40 percent increase in spending an “urgent, necessary injection of resources” to outpace America’s adversaries. He has also urged Congress to approve an additional $67 billion in funding to help cover the costs of the Iran war and other military operations around the world. Nearly all Senate Democrats blocked the request in an extraordinary act of protesting the conflict. In a move that has frustrated some Republicans, the administration split the defense budget into two buckets: $1.15 trillion that will require some Democratic support and another $350 billion meant to pass with GOP votes alone. Republicans have so far failed to agree on a strategy to pass the party-line share of funding. The gridlock has left the military vulnerable, lawmakers said. U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, estimated that as of mid-October the Iran conflict had cost more than $47 billion, forcing the Pentagon to delay trainings and maintenance projects just to cover its bills. After failing to reach a lasting ceasefire this summer, the president has threatened to restart strikes after the midterms. “Russia and China are questioning whether or not we have the resources and the ability to quickly replace dwindling stocks and ammunition,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota), who faulted Democrats for holding up the defense budget. “You’re mad at the president, but you’re taking it out on these men and women who are following orders.” Excluding the Democrats Democrats say the Trump administration is blaming them for problems of its own making. “To come in and say, ‘Oh, by the way, we made this choice and we spent all this money and we need you to replenish it’ - it takes a lot of nerve,” said Sen. Angus King (Maine), an independent who caucuses with Democrats. The Trump administration has excluded Democrats from several briefings on the $350 billion in defense spending it hopes to pass on a party-line vote. These meetings have broken a long-standing practice of sharing national security information equally with each party, lawmakers said. Multiple Republicans noted that the administration has tightened the briefings in part due to concerns about leaks to the news media, which Trump officials have blamed on congressional Democrats. Many in the GOP said they had urged the Pentagon to include both parties. “If we are asking them to make these country-altering decisions, I think we have to inform them,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer (North Dakota), one of multiple Republicans who noted they’d urged the Pentagon to share more information with Democrats. The Republican lawmaker who offered Hegseth his blunt assessment of the $1.5 trillion request also said that Democrats are partly to blame for the lack of communication. Earlier this year, the lawmaker said, he brokered a private meeting between Hegseth and a small group of Democrats. All of the Democrats declined to meet with the secretary, the lawmaker said. Other members of Congress faulted Hegseth for the distrust. In April, while appearing before the House Armed Services Committee, Hegseth delivered a broadside in his opening remarks. “The biggest adversary we face at this point,” he said, “are the reckless, feckless and defeatist words of congressional Democrats and some Republicans.” At one point during the hearing, Rep. Austin Scott (Georgia), a senior Republican on the committee, noted that the administration would need Republican and Democratic votes to secure its budget. “The way Hegseth treats people is a problem,” Scott said in an interview. ‘Shockingly unprofessional’ During Hegseth’s first private meeting with the Senate Armed Services Committee, in June 2025, he opened with a warning, according to three people familiar with his remarks. Though the hearing was classified, the secretary said, he didn’t know - and didn’t trust - everyone in the room and would watch what he said, these people recalled. They cited the exchange as an example of Hegseth’s combativeness. “It’s as shockingly unprofessional as anything I see,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who voted against Hegseth’s confirmation and has opposed the Iran war, said of the secretary’s tone. Current and former officials familiar with Hegseth’s relationships on Capitol Hill disputed assertions that the Pentagon was withholding information from Congress or refusing to meet with Democrats. They said Hegseth’s private meetings had been professional and noted that Democrats had openly attacked him, accusing him of mismanagement and dishonesty. The Pentagon did not directly address questions about this encounter or others detailed in this report. The contentious relationship has led some Republicans to ask the Pentagon to instead send uniformed officers to brief Congress, lawmakers said. Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of the Staff, has hosted private breakfasts with Republicans and Democrats at the Pentagon in an attempt to build more bipartisan support for the budget, according to lawmakers and others familiar with the sessions. A spokesperson for Caine declined to comment. Meanwhile, members of both parties voiced a sense of resignation that the defense-related committees were becoming more partisan. “Democrats don’t want to work on anything in a bipartisan way that could be construed as giving Trump a win,” said Sen. Deb Fischer (Nebraska), a senior Republican. Many Democrats said they are worried that the Pentagon’s shortfalls could hamstring military readiness for years, including in a future Democratic administration. But they argued that they need to use every tool they have to resist what they see as an unconstitutional war. “We are taking serious risks with our national security and should not be,” said Sen. Chris Coons (Delaware), the top Democrat on the Senate panel on defense spending. “At the end of the day, the president’s responsible for the decisions he’s made.” Multiple people familiar with the budget negotiations, some speaking on the condition of anonymity to provide their candid assessment, said that the Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion request was probably impossible with so little time left in the year. A U.S. official familiar with Hegseth’s relationships with lawmakers asserted that the full budget request was still viable and that Republicans, if they lose control of Congress, would see this as their last chance to secure defense-related priorities without Democratic votes. Doubts about the budget have come at a low point for Hegseth’s standing with congressional Republicans, who have signaled they will oppose his preferred picks to lead the Army and criticized him more openly in recent weeks. When the House returns in November, Hegseth will probably face an impeachment vote, led by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky), over the Iran war. Meanwhile, some Democrats felt emboldened heading into next week’s election - they appear likely to at least regain control of the House - and the prospect of launching aggressive oversight of the Pentagon. Earlier this year, Hegseth held private breakfasts with the top Republicans and Democrats on the Armed Services committees, in an effort to improve his standing. Rep. Adam Smith (Washington), the House Armed Services Committee’s top Democrat, recalled saying near the end of his meeting with Hegseth that, despite their disagreements, they didn’t have to be enemies. In an interview, Smith said he wasn’t looking to partner with “this Pentagon.” “I’m looking,” he added, “for ways to stop the awful things they’re doing with our military.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/29/inside-breakdown-trumps-15-trillion-pentagon-plan/

item.title: U.S. warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes and retaliation after elections
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States — as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter. Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by U.S. diplomats and defense officials. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over. Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon. The White House and U.S. officials declined to comment. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran “continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed” and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month — summarily rejected by Trump — that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February. The U.S. has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate — leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said. The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure. It's unclear how soon the US military would be ready While the U.S. has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated. The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the U.S. It's unclear how soon after Election Day that the U.S. military would be ready to potentially resume strikes. The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard -- roughly 9,000 troops in all -- from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region. At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003. Late Wednesday, reports emerged that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, according to a defense official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters. That official said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran. The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that's driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy. The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes. During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming “in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.” “Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?” Trump said earlier in the same address. “I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.” Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then -- especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. “Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?” he said. ___ Magdy reported from New York. AP writers Konstantin Toropin and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting. item.title: RFK Jr. eases access to unproven peptides over FDA scientists' objections
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration on Wednesday acted to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . Food and Drug Administration scientific staffers had little input on the decision and opposed the changes, according to six people familiar with its development. The draft policy posted online by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services covers a handful of injectable peptides promoted within the wellness industry for uses such as building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy. The government will take comments for two weeks before finalizing the measure. The document, primarily written by officials at HHS, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s long-standing mission of keeping unsafe health products off the U.S. market, according to the people familiar with its development. The people spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations. The policy directs the FDA not to take action against specialty pharmacies that sell a half-dozen wellness peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. Under normal FDA rules, those chemicals would be considered illegal drugs because they have not gone through the agency’s rigorous review process for safety and effectiveness. According to the document posted online, Kennedy determined the change “advances patient choice and freedom” while protecting people in the United States from peptides sold online that are often made from ingredients of unknown origin and quality. Kennedy has called himself a “big fan” of peptides and previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury. Lee Rosebush of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine said in an online post that HHS had taken “a huge step for patient and provider medical freedom.” The group, which is not a medical professional society, represents people who prescribe or sell peptides. The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers, which recently announced plans to offer wellness peptides once the government changed its policy. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth more than $2 billion. Wellness peptides are not FDA approved Some peptides occur naturally in the human body, where they trigger hormones needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss . The chemicals subject to the new policy have not been approved as safe and effective by the FDA. Still, they are promoted online by influencers and celebrities for a range of medical uses, including insomnia, anxiety, inflammatory conditions and migraines. Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official, noted that the FDA has already approved rigorously tested drugs for all of those conditions. As people “are diverted from those drugs toward this stuff, there will be more unnecessary pain and suffering,” said Lurie, who now leads the nonprofit Center for Science in the Public Interest. He also questioned the timing of the change, days before the midterm election. “This is a wink and nod to the MAHA faithful in the hope that they'll show up at the polls,” said Lurie, referring to Kennedy's “Make America Healthy Again” movement. RFK Jr. and his MAHA followers support peptides A spokesperson for HHS said the agency is “confronting the risks of black-market peptides” by giving Americans “a more controlled alternative through licensed U.S. compounders.” It is the latest example of Kennedy reshaping U.S. health policy in the MAHA mold. Some of the biggest figures in that movement sell peptide injections and supplements. The decision is a stark break from past FDA efforts to limit the availability of unproven wellness products, including peptides, stem cell therapies and dietary supplements , that make unsupported medical claims. But that approach put the agency at odds with Kennedy, who has publicly endorsed the benefits of all of those products. The policy published Wednesday is a step back from HHS' original plan, according to two of the people who discussed its development. HHS officials initially wanted the FDA to draft an official regulation that would add BPC-157 and other peptides to a list of drug substances deemed safe for use by compounding pharmacies, specialty businesses that make customized medications. FDA officials warned that the agency's scientific staffers had major safety concerns and would not support a regulation deeming the peptides safe. HHS officials moved to a different approach that directs the FDA not to enforce its rules against pharmacies that compound the substances. FDA staffers ultimately provided technical assistance in drafting the HHS plan, including guardrails intended to improve safety, such as requiring pharmacies to use peptide ingredients from FDA-registered factories. Additionally, compounders are directed to collect information on side effects for safety analysis and verify the purity of peptides they use. Lurie pointed out that the FDA, under federal law, does not have the authority to enforce those pharmacy requirements. The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, which represents specialty pharmacies, said several details need to be clarified — including when the policy takes effect and how it will intersect with state pharmacy boards, who traditionally regulate pharmacists. Decisions over compounding have long rested with the FDA, not HHS Decisions about regulating peptides and compounding pharmacies have almost always come from the FDA, which has an office dedicated to protecting U.S. consumers from unsafe or poor-quality compounded drugs. The issue of compounding safety became a greater focus for the FDA after a deadly outbreak of fungal meningitis in 2012 was linked to contaminated injections from a Massachusetts compounding pharmacy. Once a niche business, compounding has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry, providing customized medications to doctors, clinics and hospitals. It’s extremely rare for HHS to take the lead in drafting policies over the compounding industry, former FDA officials said. But federal law technically gives HHS authority over drug regulations, which are then delegated to the FDA. FDA has warned Americans about safety risks of unproven peptides Many in the U.S. who are using peptides today do not deal with a doctor or a pharmacy to get the injections, but often order vials online sold by chemical manufacturers based in China. Peptide sellers often try to skirt U.S. regulations by labeling their products as “for research use only” because the FDA does not regulate research chemicals. In 2023, the FDA added more than a dozen peptides , including BPC-157 and TB-500, to its list of substances that should not be compounded due to risks of allergic reactions, kidney damage and tumor growth. At a meeting in July , FDA staffers reiterated that more than half a dozen peptides brought forward for reconsideration remained unproven in terms of safety and effectiveness. But a panel of outside experts voted to drop restrictions on the six peptides named in Wednesday's document. The panel — selected by Kennedy’s HHS — included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org . A sign points toward voting stations inside the Arroyo Seco Regional Branch Library in Los Angeles. (Ronaldo Bolanos / Los Angeles Times) A federal judge in a blistering opinion Wednesday denied a Trump administration request to immediately block California elections officials from counting the ballots of 20,000 voters whose citizenship the administration questions. The administration swiftly said it would appeal. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter ruled that the administration’s allegations were “not credible” and that the intervention it sought would violate a host of federal laws, sow chaos in the ongoing midterm election, likely lead to the disenfranchisement of legitimate voters and foster future political meddling in elections. “This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If [the Trump administration’s] last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.” Carter, an appointee of President Clinton, wrote that never in American history “has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” and that, in bringing its suit, the Trump administration was asking the court to “believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign.” “But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter wrote. Carter’s ruling was the second to deny the Trump administration a temporary restraining order against the state and Los Angeles County this week, after a three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals denied the government’s emergency request in a separate order Monday. Carter ruled after a 3½-hour hearing Tuesday, where a slew of attorneys for the state, county and independent voting rights groups argued against the administration’s demands. Read more: Your last-minute voter guide to California's 2026 general election First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli — who is the top federal prosecutor in L.A. and argued for the Trump administration at Tuesday’s hearing — wrote on X that his office had already filed notice of appeal and “will immediately seek an emergency order” reversing Carter back in the 9th Circuit. “Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Essayli wrote. State elections officials, other state leaders, voting rights advocates and election experts all cheered the ruling. “For the second day this week, our country’s legal system is standing up to the President’s authoritarian attempts to remain in power unchecked and unchallenged,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said. “Today’s ruling is yet another important victory for the rule of law and the right to vote,” said California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta. “But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California’s elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed.” Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan, whom the Trump administration sued along with the state and Secretary of State Shirley Weber, said the ruling “reinforces what we have maintained throughout this process: election integrity and the protection of eligible voters go hand in hand.” Anna Baldwin, the director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center who argued before Carter on behalf of the NAACP and the League of United Latin American Citizens, said Carter had “affirmed what the Constitution has already made clear: The states and Congress oversee our elections, not the White House and not the Department of Justice.” Read more: Read the ballot ruling Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law, said Carter’s ruling was as sweeping a rejection of the Trump administration’s illegitimate attempts to interfere in California’s election as could possibly be written. “The federal government lost in every way it could possibly lose. It lost on the law, and it lost on the facts, and it lost on the equities — [or] weighing the harms to the various parties,” Hasen said. And that is appropriate given that the case was a “total overreach of federal power,” Hasen said. “The Constitution’s clear that states have the authority to run Congressional elections unless Congress passes a statute otherwise — and Congress didn’t do so here.” The Trump administration sued California , Weber and Logan on Oct. 15 — three months after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote a letter to Weber alleging that there may be more than 190,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California, and two days after acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter wrote again to Weber and Logan, giving them 48 hours to set aside the ballots for the 20,000 voters on the latest list. Much of the debate since has centered on the origins and evidence in support of that list. California and L.A. County officials have said the list appears to be inaccurate, with Logan’s office saying its review of a subset of about 200 voters found that a substantial portion appeared to have been born in the U.S. — a claim that has been disputed by Homeland Security officials. Elections officials from several other California counties have also raised concerns about the accuracy of smaller lists of voters derived from the 20,000 that were sent to them by Justice Department officials last week, along with a warning that they could face criminal penalties if they tabulate those votes. Officials have said the lists they received contained the names of individuals who did not appear to live in their counties or did not appear to be registered. State officials have pointed to similar lists being rejected as inaccurate elsewhere, including in Nevada. And during Tuesday’s hearing, multiple attorneys for voter advocacy groups — including the NAACP and Mi Familia en Acción — challenged both the origins and the reliability of the Trump administration’s data, and questioned why the Trump administration has so far refused to disclose when and from whom it obtained the purchased California voter roll data it says its analysis is based on. State and county officials have said that complying with the Trump administration’s demands would badly disrupt the election and could disenfranchise legitimate voters who are wrongly included on its inaccurate list. Justice Department officials have defended the list, saying it is composed of 20,000 individuals whom the administration has “high confidence” are not citizens, and that that number represents the “floor” to the issue — while the earlier, 190,000-strong list was the “ceiling” and also included people the administration had suspected but had less confidence were noncitizens. They argued that Carter should immediately bar the state and county from tabulating ballots from the flagged voters until they can prove those voters are citizens — in part because, as soon as cast ballots are received in person or removed from their envelopes, they cannot be resegregated. Essayli has said federal authorities have “overwhelming evidence” to support their claims. At Tuesday’s hearing, he said once federal authorities obtained the purchased voter registration records from the state, they “had to enrich or enhance or add, supplement, information to the voter file, so they took the info that was on there — names, addresses — and they used a database that’s often used by law enforcement, it’s used commercially.” However, in sworn court filings, other administration officials have acknowledged “discrepancies” with some of the records and noted that more recent reviews of the data did show some people on the list appear to have citizenship claims. Essayli told Carter, “We’re never going to stand here and tell you that everything is 100%.” In his ruling Wednesday, Carter also focused in part on the reliability of the list, noting that the process by which the Trump administration compiled it, and the reliability of outside databases to build it, remained unclear and could not be determined to be reliable based on the record before the court — particularly given that administration lists elsewhere have been shown to be unreliable. But Carter also touched on several other weaknesses he saw in the Trump administration’s case — weaknesses that were also hit on by the 9th Circuit panel that rejected the administration’s request Monday. Among them, Carter found that the request violates federal law precluding altering of election rules on the eve of an election. Read more: Judge in L.A. weighs feds' request to block 20,000 California votes with skepticism Carter wrote that prosecutors like Essayli can prosecute individuals who illegally vote — which he called a “clear remedy” to the administration’s concerns about illegal voters casting ballots — but that the administration’s demands to force the state and county to set aside 20,000 ballots at once “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.” “The Executive Branch cannot replace the remedy Congress carefully enacted with its own unlawful and unconstitutional solution instead,” Carter wrote. “Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” he wrote. “This Court declines to be a party to such process.” Carter also denounced the Justice Department’s letters to county elections officials threatening them with criminal penalties if they don’t comply with its demands to set the ballots aside — writing that “these threats must stop.” An appeal, if one is filed by the Trump administration, would face a “tough road ahead,” Hasen said. While not guaranteed, the appeal is likely to be taken back up by the same three-judge appellate panel who previously heard — and rejected — the administration’s emergency request to block state officials from counting the ballots. That panel — composed of two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — denied the previous request narrowly, ruling 2 to 1 that it did not have jurisdiction over the matter because Carter had not had a chance to rule in the lower court. However, both judges in the majority — Mark J. Bennett, one of the Trump appointees, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, the Biden appointee — wrote separately from the court decision to make clear that they would have denied the administration’s request on the merits too. Among other things, they wrote that the U.S. Constitution gives power over elections to the states and Congress, not the executive branch, and that federal law precludes such voting probes so close to an election. item.title: Partial Israeli election results indicate possible deadlock as Netanyahu alleges fraud
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Israeli election authorities were still counting votes from Tuesday's parliamentary election on Thursday morning. But even with the vast majority of ballots counted, it remained unclear who will form the country's new government. Neither the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor that of his prime challenger Gadi Eisenkot has an obvious course to secure a majority of seats in the Knesset, according to exit polls and partial results released by electoral authorities. As of Thursday, Israel's Central Election Committee said it had counted nearly 94% of votes. The partial results -- which are subject to some change as the rest of the votes are tallied -- indicated that Netanyahu's Likud party would win 26 seats, with Eisenkot's Yashar party on 21 seats. The CEC projected that Netanyahu's coalition was on course to secure 53 seats, slightly ahead of Eisenkot's bloc on 48 seats. Neither coalition was on course to achieve a 61-seat majority. Maya Levin,jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: This combination of pictures created on Oct. 28, 2026, shows Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot (L) addressing supporters at a rally in Tel Aviv and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressing his supporters at an election night rally in Jerusalem. Israel awaits election results as exit polls suggest close race for Netanyahu The Arab parties, meanwhile, were projected by the CEC to take 19 seats. The last stage of vote counting is expected to end on Thursday afternoon or evening local time, the CEC said. The final results will not be published until Nov. 4. If the CEC projections hold true, the two coalitions led by Netanyahu and Eisenkot may need the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties to have any chance of a majority in the Knesset. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have previously ruled out forming a coalition with the Arab parties. In his post-election speech, Netanyahu suggested that any government that included Arab parties would "endanger Israel." Arab party leaders have indicated willingness to work with the anti-Netanyahu opposition. The Arab-led Joint List -- a collection of three parties which between them were on course to win 12 seats as of Wednesday -- said in a statement that they were ready for "political cooperation to oust the Netanyahu government." Ohad Zwigenberg/AP Photo - PHOTO: An Arab woman walks with a child next to a torn Likud party campaign ad featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump, in Jerusalem on Oct. 28, 2026. No clear winner yet after polls close in Israeli elections, exit polls indicate "The Joint List will work with all its strength to bring an end to Netanyahu's rule. We are ready for political cooperation to establish an alternative government, which will present a true alternative and commit itself to a true change of the current government's racist policy," it said in a statement. Mansour Abbas, the leader of the United Arab List -- also known as Ra'am -- which was projected to win seven seats, said he had been in touch with representatives of both the Netanyahu and Eisenkot coalitions. As vote counting continued on Wednesday, Netanyahu alleged -- without providing any evidence -- that the election had been "stolen by Arab parties," claiming that Likud had gathered evidence of electoral fraud and submitted it to electoral, law enforcement and security bodies. Likud issued a statement claiming that "foreign entities" had interfered with the election by providing financial support to Arab parties. The party did not immediately provide any evidence to support its allegation. Opposition leaders condemned the prime minister's remarks, maintaining that the elections in Israel were free and fair and there was no evidence of election fraud. The Israeli police said they will investigate any credible allegations of wrongdoing. Jalaa Marey/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gestures to his supporters at the election night rally after the first exit polls were announced, in Jerusalem on Oct. 28, 2026. Dean Livne, the acting director general of the CEC said on Wednesday that there was "no basis for allegations of election theft," as reported by Israel's Kan radio station. Eisenkot, meanwhile, said on Wednesday night that he had undertaken "a long day of meetings, conversations, and preparations to realize the will of the voter." "We are focused on the heavy task entrusted to us -- bringing change to Israel," he wrote in a post to X. ABC News' Nasser Atta and Joe Simonetti contributed to this report. item.title: A suspected Chinese spy had access to Nvidia's CEO. Trump found out and didn't act.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA (Sean Gallup/Getty Images) A Chinese executive suspected of helping Beijing obtain restricted American artificial intelligence chips also developed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, raising concerns that China could gain sensitive information through her access to the technology leader. U.S. intelligence agencies concluded that the executive, Alice Huang, was gathering information for Beijing, The New York Times reported on Thursday. President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings roughly a year ago but chose not to act, according to people familiar with the classified intelligence. The discovery brought together two concerns for Washington: China's efforts to acquire advanced American chips and its potential access to the head of the company producing them. Nvidia's chips power sophisticated AI systems, making the company central to the technology competition between the United States and China. Washington has restricted exports of advanced chips to prevent Beijing from acquiring computing power that could help it match or surpass U.S. capabilities. Nvidia defended its chief executive's dealings with Alice Huang and said customers do not receive sensitive company information. "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," company spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times. Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who became a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and Nvidia customer. Toward the end of the Biden administration, the Commerce Department began investigating suspicions that Megaspeed was helping China circumvent U.S. restrictions on access to Nvidia's computing technology, the Times reported. Nvidia said its own investigation found no evidence that Megaspeed was smuggling chips. Surveillance of Alice Huang subsequently led U.S. officials to conclude she was providing information to Beijing. Her relationship with Jensen Huang raised questions about whether she could obtain sensitive information about Nvidia or Trump's thinking on chip exports, according to the report. Jensen Huang has become an influential advocate for easing restrictions on chip sales to China. Trump was wary of disrupting sales that help drive the economy and stock market or further complicating trade relations with Beijing, the Times reported. When Trump was initially briefed, officials did not believe Jensen Huang knew Alice Huang was gathering intelligence for China. The Times said it was unclear whether intelligence agencies had since changed that assessment. Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, a warning sometimes given to Americans targeted by foreign intelligence services. Such warnings can risk alerting a surveillance target, although the Times could not determine whether that concern explained the decision in this case. Rizzo said Nvidia was confident the government would notify the company if it believed someone posed a threat to American industry. Megaspeed said it retained outside counsel to investigate the allegations and informed the U.S. government that it would cooperate. Alice Huang did not respond to requests for comment, and her current role at the company remains unclear. The White House, CIA, and National Security Agency declined to comment. Chinese Embassy spokesperson Liu Chang accused the United States of pursuing "groundless smears and slanders." © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: Alaska's GOP governor orders investigation into Peltola campaign after report
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It was, for a while, considered one of those colorful quirks that crop up in the course of an election: the fact that not one but two candidates named Dan Sullivan will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot for U.S. senator from Alaska. One Dan Sullivan — Dan S. Sullivan — is the state's incumbent Republican senator. He is trying to fend off a fierce challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and secure a third term. The other Dan Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan — is a retired teacher from a tiny fishing village along the Alaska Panhandle. He has never previously campaigned for public office, and he switched his registration from "unaffiliated" to "Republican " just before the deadline to run. (He has since switched back to unaffiliated .) But now the situation seems to be getting more serious. At President Trump's direction, the Justice Department last week sued in federal court to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to siphon away votes. Then, on Wednesday, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appears to substantiate that allegation , calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot." "The Times has found, based on interviews and text messages, along with documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against the campaign, that not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader," the paper wrote. "The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory." Matthew Salisbury, a former congressional candidate and Alaska insurance manager, told the Times that he was approached by a man claiming to represent wealthy donors who wanted him to run for Senate as an independent candidate. Salisbury said he met with the man over beers at an Irish pub in Anchorage, but ultimately declined after being unable to verify his identity. “I’m not naïve," he said. In response to the report, Trump called for both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan to be removed from the ballot in a post on Truth Social . Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was ordering an investigation to determine whether the alleged effort violated state law. "Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," Dunleavy said in a statement . "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections." Sam Curtis, a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law, told CNN that the revelations in the Times report did not change the state's opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election. "Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law," Curtis said, adding that the report has "no impact on the current litigation." Yahoo The outcome of the legal dispute, if it moves forward, could have enormous national implications. Democrats need to win at least a few Senate races in historically Republican states to secure a majority in the chamber. Polls suggest Alaska is one of their best chances to turn a red seat blue. Given how close other races across the country appear to be, a legal ruling that erases a narrow Peltola victory could be the pivot point that allows the GOP to keep control of the Senate for the last two years of Trump's presidency. How did this happen, and where do things go from here? Here's everything you need to know to catch up and make sense of the story. How Alaska wound up with two Dan Sullivans on the ballot Ballot-stacking — the process of recruiting a spoiler candidate to help your candidate win — isn't unheard of in politics, and the Times says it's "generally considered legal." But it's a lot easier in Alaska than other states because of the unique way elections work there. When Peltola ran for reelection to the U.S. House in 2024, the state GOP backed an effort to help a second Democrat — an inmate who conducted his campaign from a New York prison — remain on the ballot. And during this year's primaries, super PACs aligned with both parties "flooded the state with ads for fringe candidates" in an attempt to "dilute support for the mainstream candidates opposed by the groups," according to an October Alaska Beacon report . How is any of this possible? The Last Frontier sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference. This means that candidates can claim any party affiliation on the ballot without being vetted by parties themselves. (Dan J. Sullivan initially claimed to be a Republican .) It also means that as long as they finish in the top four, primary candidates don't have to earn many votes to secure their very own ballot line on Nov. 3. (Dan J. Sullivan won 4,107 ). For months, Republicans have questioned Dan J. Sullivan's intentions and tried to get him tossed off the ballot. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court dismissed their arguments, ruling that neither state law nor the U.S. Constitution provided any legal basis for removing Dan J. Sullivan's name. How the Senate candidates will appear on Alaska's midterm ballot. elections.alaska.gov The more obscure Sullivan has "maintained that he [is] running in good faith and of his own volition, as a moderate Republican and not a secret Democrat," as a Times profile put it in August. He said he'd voted in the past for some Alaska Republicans, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski, even though he also "acknowledged previous donations to Ms. Peltola and a handful of other Democrats," and said he would prefer Peltola for Senate over the Republican incumbent "if it was between those two." But according to this week's Times report, "operatives aligned with" the Peltola campaign convinced Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race "to help Mary." The report cited as its sources 12 people "who participated in or were told of the plan" as well as interviews with other would-be recruits and dozens of internal text messages. For the record, both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which directs the party's campaign strategy in Senate races across the country, have denied any "involvement," and Dan J. Sullivan did not respond to the Times's repeated requests for comment. One of the Times's main sources — former Peltola campaign manager and longtime aide Elisa Rios, who had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit — also tried to retract her statements to the paper ahead of publication. The Times story described an elaborate endeavor — which was "internally called the ballot composition project" — that "involved secret trips to far-flung Alaskan communities and the appearance of a mysterious Midwestern operative, who traversed the state using a fake name and made his pitch to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs." The Times also reported that the "Peltola campaign's lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee" were "involved" with the effort. The Trump administration's lawsuit Legal battles over the dual Dan Sullivan issue had been confined to state courts until last week. That's when Trump's administration filed its lawsuit aiming to have the certification of the results blocked if Peltola wins a close election that may have been affected by Dan J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot. "Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election," the Department of Justice wrote in its legal filing. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump said Friday of the lawsuit . The suit argues that a Democratic victory should be considered invalid if Peltola wins by a margin smaller than the total number of votes that Dan J. Sullivan receives — under the assumption that those votes may have come from confused voters who intended to vote for the incumbent Republican senator instead. Democrats have asked the courts to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the administration lacks "any statutory or constitutional authority to insert itself" into the state's electoral process. Alaska's state government, which is currently led by Republicans, has also filed to dismiss the administration's lawsuit. On Monday, a federal judge agreed to fast-track consideration of the dispute to potentially allow it to be resolved before Election Day. Many legal experts say the lawsuit has a slim chance of success. First, it requires a very specific outcome in which Peltola wins by what would likely need to be a very thin margin. Even in that scenario, election law experts say, the appearance of confusion on the part of voters does not create legal grounds for the federal DOJ to have the results rejected. "I believe that this lawsuit is abusive in its intentions and borders on frivolous in its arguments, and that it is destined for defeat in the courts should it reach the merits," Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, told the Alaska Beacon . Nicholas Stephanopoulos, a Harvard law professor, told the Harvard Gazette that the law the administration is relying on in its lawsuit — the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — does not give federal authorities any power to challenge state election procedures. "The lawsuit has nothing to do with voter registration. There's no allegation that anybody is improperly registered in Alaska; there's no claim that Alaska isn't in compliance with the NVRA's requirements for voter registration," Stephanopoulos said. More generally, experts say the lawsuit runs against the Constitution's language granting states the power to run their own elections. "This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney who worked on voting rights cases, told Alaska Public Media . What's next? The federal judge in Alaska considering Democrats' motion to dismiss the lawsuit i ssued an order late Wednesday allowing their challenge to move forward. She gave the DOJ until Thursday afternoon to respond. That likely only matters in an extremely close race, which is not the recent norm in Alaska. The last time Dan S. Sullivan was on the ballot, he defeated his top challenger, independent candidate Al Gross, by 45,000 votes . The most recent Senate race, in 2022, was closer, but the top two finishers were both Republicans. Things are expected to be much tighter this time around. Peltola has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, but her advantage has steadily shrunk in the months leading up to Election Day. The most recent surveys have her ahead by 2 points, well within the margin for Sullivan to win. The Cook Political Report, one of the nation's most respected election forecasters, lists the race as a toss-up. Another well-regarded forecaster, the Center for Politics, categorizes it as "leans Democrat." item.title: Hegseth fires Pentagon's top military planner as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, the latest in a series of generals to be ousted and one that comes even as President Donald Trump is weighing renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. He is the second general to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the “J5,” under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced to retire last October. The defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. The move was reported earlier by The Atlantic. A spokesperson for the Joint Staff said “the Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation” and they "wish him and his family the best.” Typically, the J5 director and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president. Sylvia's firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran. Trump has vowed to “finish the job” in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said new strikes are an option after the midterm elections next week. U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action after Tuesday's elections as well as for the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter said. They say Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes. A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region . Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as the commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the J5. He is the latest in nearly two dozen generals, admirals and other military leaders to be fired, forced to retire or otherwise depart under Hegseth's tenure — almost all of which have not been publicly explained by the Pentagon. That includes the civilian secretaries of the Army and Navy as well as some top uniformed officers for the military services. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment late Wednesday. Hegseth said last month that he ordered the military to double the cuts to the overall number of top officers to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. There are currently roughly 800 flag and general officer positions. “I call it accountability and long overdue,” Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30. Some members of Congress have criticized cuts to the ranks of generals as a “purge” that will take years to rebuild. “He’s got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth, said last month. “He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it.” ___ Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani in Washington and Samy Magdy in New York contributed to this report. Alphabet ( GOOGL ) is on track for its worst day ever. The stock fell about 13% Thursday after its third quarter results , steeper than any session since it went public in 2004. That puts nearly $500 billion of stock market value on the line, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company. Only Nvidia ( NVDA ) has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Biggest one-day drops in market value for US-listed stocks, US dollars Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance Alphabet would need to close at about $274.75, down roughly 15%, to take Nvidia's record, by Yahoo Finance calculations. It's also on track for the stock's steepest drop after an earnings report since the company went public, according to Bespoke Investment Group . The previous low was a slide of nearly 10% in July 2008. Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance The quarter gave both sides plenty to argue over. But search revenue grew 12% to about $63 billion, short of Wall Street's roughly $65 billion estimate. item.title: Scientists may have found a new dwarf planet in a distant world beyond Pluto
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Scientists from the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory have announced that they have spotted a possible new dwarf planet known (for now) as 2026 ED138 orbiting the sun, located just beyond Pluto. Meet our Solar System's newest dwarf planet candidate: 2026 ED138! Orbiting past Pluto, scientists found it in NSF–DOE Rubin Observatory data from earlier in 2026. Early analysis suggests it's 600–1500 km across, one of the largest found past Neptune! 🔗 https://t.co/wTOg898zBu pic.twitter.com/hEgnk597rl — NSF-DOE Rubin Observatory (@VRubinObs) October 27, 2026 The discovery comes just months after the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which is based in Chile and funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science, began its 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in late June. The project will “relentlessly” photograph the southern sky over the next 10 years, creating a time-lapse of the universe, allowing scientists to spot objects that move or change and potentially uncover previously unknown objects in the solar system . What Do We Know About 2026 ED138? 2026 ED138 was found by Matthew Holman, of the Center for Astrophysics (CfA), while he was examining observations collected by the Rubin observatory earlier this year. On October 13, Holman ran the observations through computer software designed to find distant objects moving across the sky. Holman said, “my first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” adding that “objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.” Newsweek has reached out to Holman for comment. After the potential discovery emerged, scientists trawled back through the catalog of Rubin images, taken from March to July, and were able to find the object in more than 20 observations. A mosaic of images captured by NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory of the newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 (ED138) Its distance places it beyond Pluto’s orbit, and early estimates indicate that it could be one of the largest and brightest objects that’s ever been found in that distant part of the solar system. Scientists estimate that ED138 could be between about 600 and 1,500 kilometers (370 to 930 miles) across, based on its distance, brightness and estimates of how much light its surface reflects. Objects that are that big are expected to be rounded by their own gravity, an important requirement for an object to be considered a dwarf planet, however more observations will be needed to establish its true size and determine whether it qualifies. ED138 is currently around 46 times further from the sun than Earth is, putting it further out into the solar system than Pluto’s average distance, which is roughly 40 times further from the sun than Earth is. Its location may also help explain why such a large object has remained undetected. ED138 appears against a crowded part of the sky near the plane of the Milky Way, where huge numbers of stars can make moving objects difficult to identify. Thousands of New Objects Already Found A model of the inner Solar System showing the asteroids discovered by Rubin in light teal. Known asteroids are dark blue. The potential dwarf planet is the latest addition to a rapidly growing list of solar system objects discovered using Rubin data. Remarkably, more than 11,000 new asteroids were discovered before the main 10-year survey had even started. In April, the observatory announced that scientists had submitted around 1 million observations to the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center, covering more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids as well as over 80,000 known objects. The unknown objects included 33 previously unknown near-Earth objects (NEOs), none of which presented a threat to Earth, as well as hundreds of objects beyond Neptune. The observations came from Rubin’s earlier testing and optimization work rather than the main survey. Rubin scientists described the April asteroid haul as “just the tip of the iceberg.” A 10-Year Map of the Changing Sky The scale of the observatory’s work is set to grow considerably. Rubin’s main survey officially began on June 30, 2026. Over the next decade, the observatory will scan the southern sky, producing hundreds of images each night and revisiting areas of the sky again and again. The observatory is expected to collect huge amounts of data as it repeatedly photographs the sky, eventually building up around 30 million gigabytes of information over its lifetime. One of its major goals is to create a much more complete inventory of the solar system, alongside studying the Milky Way and investigating dark matter and dark energy “to grasp the fundamental laws that govern our existence,” Darío Gil, under secretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy says. That means ED138 may prove significant not only because of what it is, but because of what its discovery suggests may still be hiding in the distant solar system. With Rubin photographing the sky for the next 10 years, scientists will have opportunities to spot faint and moving objects that were missed by earlier searches. If ED138 is eventually confirmed as a dwarf planet, its discovery may be one of the first major examples of the new worlds Rubin can uncover. item.title: Manhunt grows for escaped killer who may have left area where truck was ditched
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jacob Morley, a convicted killer on the loose since Sunday, has no known connection to the small Illinois town where the truck he is accused of stealing was found, the police chief said Wednesday. “What we have seen kind of leads us in the direction that he’s not still here. But that doesn’t mean that we’ve stopped looking,” Marion Police Chief David Fitts said. Morley, 28, convicted of killing a co-worker in 2022 , was serving a life sentence when he escaped from Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, sometime before 11:30 p.m. Sunday, officials there said. Morley had stolen a work truck, and early Tuesday that truck was found behind a business in Marion, a town of around 16,000 that is around 100 miles north of Tiptonville, authorities in Marion and Tennessee said. Security video captured Morley driving away in a flatbed truck. There have been no reports in Marion of any other stolen vehicles, and there was no evidence around the truck that was found, Fitts said. There have also been no confirmed sightings, he said. “There’s really nowhere for him to go here where he wouldn’t be recognized. His face is all over the news,” Fitts said. Morley has no known connection to Marion or southern Illinois, he said. “Have no idea why he would come here, other than I-57 is a major interstate and it runs right through the middle of our town,” Fitts said. “And I don’t know, maybe he was low on gas and just pulled off. I don’t know.” Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary after a trial in February 2025. He also pleaded guilty to theft of property. He was accused of shooting Cody Birchfield in the back of the head in 2022, according to court documents. Birchfield’s body was found in a large metal box under Morley’s residence, the documents say. Birchfield’s sister, Carrie Norman, said Wednesday that “it feels like a scary movie.” The family, she said, “have to go back through the experience — once again. Once again, because you don’t know where he’s at, but you know what he’s capable of.” Also Wednesday, the reward for information leading to Morley’s arrest increased from $2,500 to $15,000, a combined sum from the Tennessee governor’s office, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Marshals Service, the bureau said. Fitts said he wished Morley had been caught, but he urged people not to take things into their own hands. “This is really frustrating that we can’t find him. Somebody will eventually, I have no doubt in my mind. I wish it was us so we could catch him now,” Fitts said. “But, and I just want to let our people know that, again, don’t approach him. Call 911. We’ll handle it.” Around 11:30 p.m. Sunday, prison staff members confirmed that Morley was unaccounted for and conducted an emergency count and search of the facility, the Tennessee Department of Correction said. Security video showed Morley “breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform,” the department said. The department has not given more details about how the escape occurred, which it said Wednesday is under investigation.
